2.3. From noisy values to noisy choices

On each trial the decision maker compares noisy estimates of the two values. As in the original implementation of the model, we write the estimate of option j as Vj = D j (r j +η j ) with independent η j ∼ N (0, σ 2 ε,j ), and assume that the larger estimate is chosen. Then

Strictly, the signal model of Eq. ( 1) gives each estimate a variance of t j σ 2 ε,j ; the original implementation, which we follow in the main analyses, omits the delay factor. Because delays are held fixed when the stakes are rescaled, both versions lead to the same elasticities in Proposition 2, and we fit the delay-scaled version as a robustness check (Section 4.9).

The sensitivity α is therefore not a free parameter. It is fully determined by the attention parameter β, the amounts, the delays and the prior variance σ 2 u . Allowing for occasional lapses with probability ϵ gives the choice rule in Eq. ( 9) below. We call this model R².

2.4. Testable predictions

To describe how a quantity f depends on the stakes, we use its elasticity with respect to a common rescaling of both amounts, r j ↦ → λr j , with delays and σ 2 u held fixed:

An elasticity of e means that f grows approximately as λ e . The quantity that governs how consistent choices are is the argument of Φ, which we call the effective precision, z = α ∆V . A larger |z| means a more predictable choice.

Proposition 1 (Magnitude effect on discounting). Under R², E[k j ] = -1 for every option. Equivalently, in the descriptive parameterisation log k j = c k -m k log r j , rational inattention implies m k = 1.

Proposition 2 (Magnitude dependence of choice precision). Under R², define the weights each of which sums to 1 over the two options.

Then , with E[α] → 1 2 when discounting is weak (D j → 1); and (ii) whenever the two options are discounted equally, D SS = D LL , the effective precision has elasticity exactly E[z] = 3 2 , for any amounts, delays, β and σ 2 u.

In words: rational inattention predicts that the effective precision of choices grows with the stakes approximately as λ 3/2 . When all amounts are multiplied by nine, choices should become about 91.5 = 27 times more precise. Part (ii) shows that this prediction does not depend on the particular values of the free parameter. We confirmed numerically that it holds closely in the real designs analysed here: across all 337,672 trials of the 39 pooled studies, evaluated at each participant's fitted β, the median of E[z] was 1.50, and the median of the study medians was 1.49 (range 1.18-1.76).

Proposition 3 (Coupling of the two magnitude effects). (3

Generalise Eq

Both magnitude slopes are therefore driven by the same participant-specific quantity γ i . In the weak-discounting limit (D ij → 1), E[α i ] = γ i /2 = m k,i /2, so that the two slopes are perfectly correlated across participants.

In words: if one attentional mechanism produces both magnitude effects, people who show a stronger magnitude effect in discounting must also show a correspondingly stronger magnitude effect in the precision of their choices. This is the prediction that we test with the participant-level correlation between m k and m α . The correspondence with the H2 slopes is exact only in the weak-discounting limit; with stronger discounting the two slopes remain linearly related within a design, but the factor linking them depends on the discount factors, so the test is of a strong positive association rather than of a specific slope.

Proposition 4 (Interpretation of the free noise slope).

R² is the special case g1 = 0, and g 1 is the amount by which the elasticity of effective precision departs from the rational-inattention prediction.

Together, Propositions 1-4 give four quantitative tests: the discount-rate slope should be m k = 1; effective precision should grow with elasticity close to 3/2; the free noise slope should be g1 = 0; and the two magnitude slopes should be tightly linked across participants.

3. Methods

>Methods

3.1. Data

We used the ITC Database (Pongratz and Schoemann, 2026, 2025), which contains 100 datasets with 11,852 participants and 1,172,644 trials. We first applied the exclusions recorded in the database, that is, the participants and trials that the original authors had flagged. We then removed trials with a non-positive SS amount, trials in which the LL amount was not larger than the SS amount, and trials in which the LL option was not later than the SS option. Finally, we removed participants with fewer than 10 remaining trials. All delays were converted to days and all amounts were kept in their original currency. This left 986,281 trials from 10,513 participants in 109 study-by-subset units. We refer to these units as studies.

3.1.1. Selecting studies in which magnitude varies

To learn how discounting and noise depend on reward magnitude, a study must vary the amount on offer, and this variation must not simply be a by-product of changes in the ratio between the two amounts or in the delay. For each study we therefore regressed the log SS amount on the log LL/SS ratio and the log delay, and kept studies in which the remaining variation in the log amount spanned at least a factor of two (from the 5th to the 95th percentile). Forty-one studies met this criterion. One of them (Thrailkill 2022b; 427 participants with 27 choices each) could not be fitted by any of the models within the available computing time and was excluded before analysis. A second (Weidacker 2020; 14 participants) was fitted and reported but left out of all pooled estimates because of its very small sample. The pooled analyses therefore cover 39 studies from 35 papers (Fig. 2).

3.2. Models

All three models share the choice rule of Gershman and Bhui (2020):

Here r j and t j are the amount and the delay of option j, V j is its discounted value, Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and α is the sensitivity of choices to the value difference. A large α means precise, nearly deterministic choices, and a small α means noisy choices. The lapse rate ϵ allows for occasional random responses. It was shared by all participants of a study and given a Beta(1, 20) prior, which favours small values. The models differ only in how k and α in Eq. ( 9) depend on the amounts.

3.2.1. H2: a descriptive model

In H2 the discount rate of each option depends on its own amount, and the sensitivity depends on the total amount at stake:

The slope m k is the size of the magnitude effect on discounting: m k = 0 means no magnitude effect, and m k = 1 means that the discount rate is inversely proportional to the amount. The slope m α describes how the sensitivity per currency unit changes with the stakes. Because the value difference between the options itself grows in proportion to the amounts, m α = 0 means that choices become more precise as the stakes rise, and m α = -1 means that choices are equally precise at every magnitude. Log amounts were centred within each study, which does not change the slopes.

3.2.2. R²: rational inattention

In R² (Section 2), following Gershman and Bhui (2020), where D j = 1/(1 + k j t j ) is the discount factor of option j, σ 2 ε,j is the noise in the internal estimate of option j, and σ 2 u is the variance of all amounts that the participant has seen up to the current trial (with a floor of 10 -5 ), which stands for the participant's learned expectation of how variable rewards are.

A single parameter per participant, the attention parameter β, therefore determines both the discount rate and the noise. R² implies m k = 1 (Proposition 1) and an effective precision of choices, α times the value difference, that grows approximately as r 3/2 (Proposition 2).

3.2.3. R2F: rational inattention with a free noise slope R2F multiplies the sensitivity of R² by exp

)︁ , with the log total amount centred within each study. R² is the special case g0 = g1 = 0. The slope g 1 therefore measures directly how far the dependence of choice noise on magnitude departs from the rational-inattention prediction. A negative g 1 means that choices become precise more slowly as the stakes rise than rational inattention predicts. R2F keeps the discounting part of R² unchanged.

3.2.4. Hierarchical structure and priors

Let θ i ∈ R P be the parameter vector of participant i in a study (for H2,

Within each study, participants were modelled as draws from a multivariate normal population, so that θ i ∼ N (︁ µ, diag(σ) Ω diag(σ) )︁ .

This non-centred form samples more efficiently than drawing θ i directly (Gelman et al., 2013). The priors were where N + is the half-normal distribution and the LKJ(2) prior mildly favours weak correlations (Lewandowski et al., 2009).

The prior means and scales were weakly informative: for H2, (a p ) = (-4, 0.5, a α , 0) and (b p ) = (3, 1, 3, 1), with a α = log 3 -log r SS placing the typical sensitivity on the scale of the study's amounts, and (s p ) = (1.5, 0.5, 1.5, 0.5); for R², µ log β ∼ N (4 -log r SS , 4 2 ) and s = 1.5; for R2F, the same prior for log β and µ g0 ∼ N (0, 2 2 ), µ g1 ∼ N (0, 1), with (s p ) = (1.5, 1, 0.5). With y n ∈ {0, 1} denoting the choice on trial n (1 = LL) and i(n) its participant, the joint posterior of a study is where P n is the choice probability of Eq. ( 9) evaluated at θ i(n) .

The hierarchical structure lets participants with few or uninformative choices borrow strength from the rest of their study. Units below the 2× threshold were not analysed.

3.2.5. Short questionnaires

Seventeen studies collected fewer than 60 choices per participant (median), most often with the 27-item Monetary Choice Questionnaire (Kirby et al., 1999). Such data contain too little information to estimate a separate magnitude slope for every participant. For these studies, the main analysis estimated the slopes (m k and m α in H2, and g 1 in R2F) once per study while keeping participant-specific intercepts ("pooled-slope" versions of the models), with the same priors as the corresponding population means. The full models with participant-specific slopes were also fitted wherever this was possible and are reported as sensitivity analyses.

3.3. Inference

The models were written in PyMC (Abril-Pla et al., 2023) and sampled with the No-U-Turn sampler (Hoffman and Gelman, 2014) implemented in NumPyro (Phan et al., 2019). Diagnostics and cross-validation were computed with ArviZ (Kumar et al., 2019). Each fit used C = 4 chains with 1,500 warm-up and S = 1,500 retained draws per chain and a target acceptance rate of 0.95. In a few large datasets a chain occasionally settled in a clearly worse region of the parameter space. Writing lc = S -1 ∑︁ s ∑︁ n log p(y n | θ (c,s) ) for the mean log-likelihood of chain c, we discarded, and counted, every chain with lc < max c ′ lc ′ -50. Convergence was assessed with the rank-normalised split-ˆ︁ R (Vehtari et al., 2021). A fit was flagged as poorly converged if any reported parameter had ˆ︁ R > 1.01, if more than one chain was discarded, or if ˆ︁ R could not be computed. Flagged fits were kept in the main analyses, and all pooled results are also reported for well-converged studies only.

3.4. Model comparison

Models were compared within each study by their expected accuracy in predicting new choices, measured by the expected log pointwise predictive density for a new trial, where ϑ collects all parameters and y -n is the data without trial n.

We estimated Eq. ( 15) by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO; Vehtari et al., 2017). For posterior draws ϑ (s) , s = 1, . . . , S, the raw importance ratios ρ (s) n = 1/p(y n | ϑ (s) ) are stabilised by replacing their largest values with the order statistics of a fitted generalised Pareto distribution, giving weights w(s) n , and

The estimated shape parameter kn of the Pareto fit serves as a diagnostic of reliability. For two models A and B fitted to the same trials, we report the paired difference and its standard error, and, to compare studies of different sizes, the difference per 1,000 choices, 1000 ∆elpd LOO /N .

This measure rewards a model for predicting held-out choices and so automatically penalises unnecessary flexibility.

3.5. Combining results across studies

Let ŷs be the estimate from study s = 1, . . . , K (a posterior mean) and v s its sampling variance (the squared posterior standard deviation). We used the random-effects model ŷs = θ s + e s , e s ∼ N (0, v s ), with the DerSimonian-Laird estimate of the between-study variance (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986), where μFE = ∑︁ s w s ŷs / ∑︁ s w s .

The pooled estimate and its standard error are μ = and heterogeneity is summarised by (Higgins and Thompson, 2002).

Correlations were pooled on the Fisher scale, ζ = tanh -1 (r), with deltamethod variance Var(ζ) ≈ v r /(1 -r 2 ) 2 , and transformed back.

For moderator analyses we extended Eq. ( 18) to a metaregression, θ s = x ⊤ s b + u s , where x s contains an intercept and one moderator. The between-study variance was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (Viechtbauer, 2005), that is, by minimising with b = (X ⊤ WX) -1 X ⊤ Wŷ.

Confidence intervals used the Knapp-Hartung adjustment (Knapp and Hartung, 2003), with t quantiles on K -p degrees of freedom.

Because the REML estimator differs slightly from DerSimonian-Laird, the all-study estimates in the moderator analysis differ slightly from the main pooled estimates (for example, m k = 0.74 rather than 0.70); all main results are reported with DerSimonian-Laird. The p-values of the 30 moderator tests were adjusted with the Holm procedure (Holm, 1979): with ordered p-values p (1) ≤ • • • ≤ p (M ) , the adjusted value is p(m) = max l≤m min{1, (M -l + 1) p (l) }.

3.6. Posterior predictive checks

Following recommended practice for computational modelling (Palminteri et al., 2017; Wilson and Collins, 2019), we did not rely on model comparison alone. For every trial we computed the posterior-mean predicted probability pn and compared it with the observed choices. Overall accuracy was summarised by the Brier score, N -1 ∑︁ n (y n -pn ) 2 , and by the mean absolute calibration error, B -1 ∑︁ B b=1 |ȳ b -pb | over B = 20 quantile bins of pn . To test whether each model captures how choice sharpness changes with the stakes, we fitted, within each within-study quintile q of the total amount, the logistic calibration model

A slope b q = 1 means correctly calibrated sharpness, and b q > 1 means that the observed choices are sharper than predicted. Rational inattention passes this test only if b q is constant across magnitude quintiles.

3.7. Model recovery and robustness

To check that the comparison can favour R² when R² is true, we generated synthetic data on the real trials of six studies, using each participant's posterior-mean log β and the study's posterior-mean lapse rate, and refitted all three models to ỹ with the same methods.

Finally, to check that the conclusions do not depend on the form of the choice rule, we refitted all three models in the same six studies with (i) a logistic link, P (LL) = (1 -ϵ) σ(α ∆V ) + ϵ/2 with σ(x) = 1/(1 + e -x ), and (ii) one lapse rate per participant, logit ϵ i = µ ϵ + σ ϵ ξ i with ξ i ∼ N (0, 1), µ ϵ ∼ N (-3, 1) and σ ϵ ∼ N + (0, 1). Analyses were run in Python on a laptop computer and on cloud CPU notebooks.

4. Results

>Results

4.1. Letting choice noise scale freely improves fit in every study

Rational inattention in its pure form (R²) was the worstfitting model in every study (Fig. 3). Freeing the dependence of choice noise on magnitude (R2F) improved predictive accuracy in all 37 studies in which both models could be compared (total ∆elpd LOO = +13,233, SE 177; median per study +199). Even the smallest improvement in a single study (12.7) was more than twice its standard error. The two remaining studies (Cao 2021 Exp. 2, subset 1, and Robinson 2015) could not enter comparisons involving R2F, because the leave-one-out estimate of R2F was not finite for one and two of their trials, respectively (and in Robinson 2015 three of four chains were also discarded). H2 still outperformed R² in both studies, by 1,808 and 668 elpd LOO units. Per-study estimates and model comparisons are listed in

Table A.1 (Appendix A). The descriptive H2 model outperformed R² in all 39 studies (total ∆elpd LOO = +23,854, SE 213) and R2F in 31 of 37 (total +8,145, SE 134), and R2F was not reliably better than H2 in any study. In short, the single parameter that rational inattention uses for both discounting and noise is not enough, and most of what is missing concerns noise.

4.2. The magnitude effect on discounting is robust but smaller than predicted

Larger rewards were discounted less in 35 of 39 studies (94% highest-density interval of the study-level m k above zero; Fig. 4a). The pooled slope was m k = 0.70 [0.59, 0.82] across all studies and 0.58 [0.42, 0.73] across the 26 wellconverged studies, with large differences between studies (I² = 0.98). Both estimates are clearly below the value of 1 implied by k ∝ 1/(βr). The magnitude effect is therefore real and general, but it is weaker than rational inattention requires.

4.3. Choice precision rises much more slowly with the stakes than rational inattention predicts

Choice sensitivity per currency unit decreased with magnitude (Fig. 4b): m α = -0.74 [-0.91, -0.58] across all studies and -0.68 [-0.77, -0.58] across well-converged studies.

It was negative in 33 of 39 studies and positive in none.

Because the value difference grows with the stakes, the effective precision of choices, z = α ∆V , still rose with magnitude, but only weakly. Computed exactly on the real designs with Eq. ( 7) and each participant's fitted parameters, the elasticity E[z] had a median (across studies) of 0.31 under H2 and 0.34 under R2F, compared with 1.49 under R² (Proposition 2). In other words, when the stakes increase ninefold, rational inattention predicts that choices become about 27 times more precise (9 1.5 ), whereas the data show an increase of only about twofold (90.31 ≈ 2.0). The free noise slope in R2F measures this gap directly: g1 = -1.10 [-1.21, -0.99] across all studies and -1.17 [-1.28, -1.05] across well-converged studies, negative in 35 of 39 studies (Fig. 5). This value is close to the difference between the H2 estimate of m α and the value of about +0.5 implied by R², as expected from Proposition 4 if both models describe the same pattern in the data.

4.4. The two magnitude effects are not coupled as the theory requires

Proposition 3 implies two tests of the link between the magnitude effects. The first concerns their average values. Under rational inattention, and its generalisation with a free attention elasticity, the magnitude slope of sensitivity should be positive and about half the slope of discounting (m α ≈ m k /2 ≈ +0.35 for the observed m k ). Instead, m k was reliably positive in 35 of 39 studies (reliably negative in 2), whereas m α was reliably negative in 33 and reliably positive in none (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). The sensitivity slope therefore had the opposite sign to the one the coupling requires. The second test concerns individual differences: if one attentional mechanism produced both effects, participants with a stronger magnitude effect in discounting should also show a stronger magnitude effect in choice noise.

Across the 23 studies in which participant-specific slopes could be estimated, the population correlation between m k and m α was small and not reliably different from zero (pooled r = 0.14 [-0.04, 0.31]; 0.08 [-0.11, 0.27] in wellconverged studies; Fig. 6b). Across studies, the study-level means were weakly related when all studies were included (r = 0.32, k = 39; Fig. 6a), but this relation disappeared among well-converged studies (r = 0.04, k = 26). It was driven by flagged fits, notably Andersen 2014 and Zhao 2019. This second test, however, has limited power in these designs. To check it, we simulated data from H2 on the real trials of four well-converged studies (Cao 2021 Exp. 2 subset 2, Kräplin 2020b, Zgonnikov 2019 and Stevens 2016), using each study's fitted population parameters but setting the correlation between m k and m α to 0.78-0.88. Fitting the same model recovered correlations of only -0.04 to 0.66 (mean 0.32), with wide intervals. Participant-level magnitude slopes are therefore estimated too noisily, and shrunk too strongly towards the population mean, for the correlation to be a sensitive test. The weak observed correlation is consistent with a modest or absent link but cannot by itself rule out a strong one; the evidence against coupling rests mainly on the opposite signs of the average slopes.

4.5. Posterior predictive checks locate the misfit in how choice sharpness changes with the stakes

We compared posterior-mean predictions with the observed choices for all 337,672 trials of the 39 pooled studies (Fig. 7). H2 was best calibrated overall (mean absolute calibration error over 20 quantile bins, 1.3 percentage points; Brier score 0.091), followed by R2F (2.0 points; 0.102) and R² (3.2 points; 0.112). R² systematically over-predicted larger-later choices in the middle of the probability range. The decisive question for rational inattention, however, is whether a model gets the sharpness of choices right at each magnitude. We therefore regressed the observed choices on the predicted log-odds separately within each within-study magnitude quintile. A slope of 1 means correctly calibrated sharpness, and a slope above 1 means that the observed choices are sharper than predicted. For R², this slope fell steeply with magnitude, from 1.46 (SE 0.01) for the smallest stakes to 0.98 (0.01) for the largest. R² is thus far too noisy for small rewards relative to large ones, because it lets precision grow too quickly with the stakes. H2 and R2F, which estimate this dependence freely, had nearly constant slopes (H2: 1.12-1.16; R2F: 1.12-1.20). Their common offset above 1 reflects averaging over posterior uncertainty and is the same at every magnitude.

4.6. Sampling difficulties do not explain the poor fit of R²

Several large datasets, either with short questionnaires or with very many trials per participant, were hard to sample. Fourteen of 40 main H2 fits, 17 of 40 R2F fits and 32 of 40 R² fits were flagged, about half of each set only mildly ( ˆ︁ R ≤ 1.05). Severe problems were concentrated in six datasets (Andersen 2014 , Thrailkill 2023 , Rodriguez-Moreno 2021 , Robinson 2015 , Cao 2021 Exp. 2 subset 1 and Alvarez 2022). Our conclusions do not depend on these fits. The differences in model comparison are large in every study, and pooled estimates restricted to wellconverged studies lead to the same conclusions. Fitting the full H2 model with participant-specific slopes to the 34 studies in which this was feasible gave the same pooled slopes (m k = 0.59 [0.50, 0.69], m α = -0.72 [-0.95, -0.48]). We also refitted six severely flagged R² fits (Chiong 2016 , Civai 2016 , Gluth 2017 Exp. 2, Lempert 2017b , Zhang 2022 and Zhou 2022) with twice the warm-up (3,000 iterations) and a target acceptance rate of 0.99. Only one flag was resolved (Chiong 2016, ˆ︁ R = 1.00); the others remained flagged ( ˆ︁ R 1.02-1.44, or more than one chain discarded).

In every case the refitted R² still fitted clearly worse than R2F (by 50-508 elpd LOO units). In these studies the R² chains settled in modes 30-130 log-likelihood units apart, and R² compensated for its misfit by inflating the lapse rate (median ϵ = 0.08 compared with 0.02 under H2; larger than under H2 in 36 of 40 studies). This pattern points to a misspecified model rather than to a failure of the sampler. Because only the chains in the best mode were retained, the predictive accuracy of R² is, if anything, overstated, and the model comparisons are conservative. As a check that does not depend on Markov chain Monte Carlo at all, we also fitted R² and R2F separately to every participant by maximum likelihood (with a perparticipant lapse rate and several starting points; 5,729 participants in the 39 pooled studies). The participantlevel noise slope was again negative: its median was below zero in 35 of 39 studies, and the random-effects pooled mean was g1 = -0.66 [-0.89, -0.42]. Without hierarchical pooling the two extra parameters per participant are costly, and the evidence depended on the penalty for complexity: R2F was favoured by AIC in total (by 8,980 units) and in 25 of 39 studies, whereas BIC, which penalises extra 0 1 2 3 4 5 Study-level mean slope (94% HDI) Bixter 2017 • Zhou 2022 • Faulkner 2014 Thome 2023 (1) Yang 2022 (2) Cao 2021 Exp2 (1) Scherbaum 2018a Hartmann 2020 • Robinson 2015 Yang 2022 (1) Rodriguez-Moreno 2021 Bixter 2019 • Lempert 2016 Gluth 2017 Exp2 Lempert 2017b Lempert 2015 Thome 2023 (2) Castrellon 2019 Zilker 2021 Civai 2016 • Zgonnikov 2019 • Linhartova 2020 Cao 2021 Exp2 (2) • Thrailkill 2022a • Thrailkill 2023 • Stevens 2016 Ortner 2013 • Gluth 2017 Exp1 Keidel 2024 (1) • Keidel 2022 • Reppert 2015 Chiong 2016 Keidel 2024 (2) • Alvarez 2022 Zhang 2022 Kräplin 2020b • Berenson 2016 • Zhao 2019 Andersen 2014 • Pooled: all studies Pooled: converged only • short questionnaire: slopes estimated once per study (pooled-slope H2) a Discount-rate slope m k converged flagged (r̂r̂ > 1.01) -3 -2 -1 0 1 Study-level mean slope (94% HDI) scale-free noise constant α b Sensitivity slope m α parameters more heavily, favoured R² in 25 studies, mainly the short questionnaires with 27 choices per person.

This is exactly the situation in which hierarchical estimation, which borrows strength across participants, is needed; it confirms that the negative noise slope is not an artefact of the sampler.

4.7. The methods favour rational inattention when it is true

A flexible model can win a comparison simply because it is flexible. To check that our comparison can favour R² when R² is true, we simulated choices from R² for six studies that span the range of design sizes (Keidel 2024, Berenson 2016, Castrellon 2019, Bixter 2019, Yang 2022 and Scherbaum 2018a; 852 to 7,087 trials). Each simulation used the real trials and each participant's running reward variance, together with each participant's posterior-mean log β and the study's posterior-mean lapse rate from the R² fit to the real data. We fitted R², R2F and H2 to the simulated data with exactly the same methods (pooled-slope versions for the three short questionnaires) and compared them by PSIS-LOO (Table 1). R2F did not gain over R² on data generated by R². The R² -R2F difference ranged from -7.5 to +4.4 elpd LOO units and was within two standard errors of zero in five of the six studies; in the sixth (Yang 2022), R² was ahead by 4.4 (SE 1.0). The recovered noise slope was close to its true value of zero: in every study the 94% highest-density interval of g 1 included zero (point estimates -0.23 to 0.59). H2 did not outperform R² on these data either. R² was clearly ahead in the three larger designs (by 53, 128 and 352 units), and the two models were within 1.5 standard errors of each other in the three smaller designs. On the real data, by contrast, R2F beat R² in the same six studies by 13 to 320 units, and H2 beat R² by 14 to 564 units. The advantages of the magnitude-dependent models on the real data are therefore not an artefact of extra flexibility or of the methods. 4.8. The failure of rational inattention holds across study designs

The studies differed considerably in all three slopes (I² = 89-98%). We therefore asked whether study design explains these differences, and whether the failure of rational inattention is limited to particular kinds of study. For each outcome (m k , m α , g 1 , and the R2F -R² and H2 -R2F differences in elpd LOO per 1,000 choices) we fitted randomeffects meta-regressions with one moderator at a time. The moderators were taken from the database records and the study designs: potentially real versus hypothetical rewards (21 vs. 18 studies), online versus laboratory testing (9 vs. 30), time pressure (13 vs. 26), the Kirby questionnaire versus other procedures (8 vs. 31), the width of the magnitude range, and the number of choices per participant.

No moderator survived correction for multiple tests (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.11). The largest uncorrected effects were a larger R2F advantage in studies with a wider magnitude range (+12.3 elpd LOO per 1,000 choices per log unit, p = 0.004), which is expected if the misfit of R² grows with the range of stakes, and a more negative m α under time pressure (-0.35, p = 0.009). More importantly, the central result held in every subgroup (Fig. 8). The noise slope g 1 was clearly negative in all eight subgroups (pooled estimates -0.83 to -1.16, every 95% CI excluding zero). The sensitivity slope m α (-0.64 to -1.00) was far below the value of about +0.5 implied by R² in every subgroup, and the discount-rate slope m k ranged from 0.58 to 0.89. The misfit of rational inattention is therefore not a by-product of hypothetical rewards, online samples, time pressure or questionnaire designs.

4.9. The conclusions do not depend on the choice rule

We refitted the models in the six model-recovery studies with a logistic instead of a probit choice rule, with a separate lapse rate for every participant, and with choice noise that grows with delay as in the signal model of Eq. ( 1) (R² and R2F only). In both variants R2F beat R² in all six studies, by more than two standard errors (logistic rule: 10.7 to 354.0 elpd LOO units; per-participant lapses: 13.5 to 299.9), and H2 beat R² in all six (12.3 to 619.9 and 15.0 to 575.3). The noise slope stayed clearly negative (g 1 from -0.91 to -1.39 with the logistic rule and from -0.91 to -1.60 with per-participant lapses, compared with -0.90 to -1.42 in the main fits), and m k and m α changed by at most 0.05 and 0.07. With delay-scaled choice noise, R2F again beat R² in all six studies by more than two standard errors (11.0 to 406.4 elpd LOO units), the noise slope remained negative (g 1 from -0.47 to -1.12), and H2 still fitted better than R² in all six (9.6 to 597.5; in the smallest study by 1.9 standard errors). The failure of the rational-inattention noise prediction is therefore not a consequence of the probit link, of the shared lapse rate, or of omitting the delay from the choice noise. 5. Discussion

We asked whether a single attentional resource, as proposed by rational inattention, can explain both why people discount small rewards more steeply and why their choices become more consistent as the stakes rise. Across 39 independent intertemporal-choice studies with 5,729 participants, the magnitude effect on discounting was robust, but the rational-inattention account of Gershman and Bhui (2020) did not capture how choice noise changes with the stakes. Allowing choice noise to change freely with magnitude improved out-of-sample prediction in every study. Choice sensitivity per currency unit fell as the stakes rose, whereas the theory requires it to rise. The magnitude slope of sensitivity also had the opposite sign to the one implied by the coupling of the two effects. Model recovery, posterior predictive checks, moderator analyses and refits with different choice rules all pointed the same way. We discuss what these results mean for rational inattention, for the magnitude effect, and for models of intertemporal choice more generally.

5.1. Choice noise does not scale as rational inattention predicts

The central failure concerns choice noise. Rational inattention ties the precision of choices to the precision of the internal representation of each reward. If large rewards receive more attention, they are represented more precisely, and choices between them should be much less noisy. In the model of Gershman and Bhui (2020), this link is not a side assumption; it follows from the same equations that produce the magnitude effect on discounting. The data show a very different pattern. Choices did become somewhat more consistent as the stakes rose, but only slightly: the effective precision grew roughly as the cube root of the stakes (E[z] ≈ 0.3), whereas the model requires growth with the 1.5th power (Proposition 2). Put simply, when the stakes rise ninefold, the theory expects choices to become about 27 times more precise, and people became only about twice as precise.

Three features of the results make this conclusion hard to dismiss. First, the improvement from freeing the noise slope was not confined to a few large or unusual datasets: it appeared in all 37 studies, with a consistently negative slope. Second, the posterior predictive checks showed exactly where R² goes wrong. Its errors are systematic: it predicts choices that are too noisy for small rewards and too sharp for large ones, and this pattern disappears once the noise slope is free. Third, the simulations showed that our methods do not favour the more flexible models when rational inattention is true. The advantage of R2F on real data is therefore not an artefact of extra parameters, which is a common concern when complex models are compared (Navarro, 2019; Wilson and Collins, 2019).

The relation between the two magnitude effects is a separate problem for the account (Proposition 3). If one attentional resource produced both effects, the magnitude slope of sensitivity should be positive and proportional to the magnitude slope of discounting. On average, the two slopes instead had opposite signs in almost every study. The participant-level correlation between them was weak, but our simulations showed that this test has little power in existing designs, so we do not treat it as strong evidence. Taken together, the results suggest that the magnitude effect on discounting and the magnitude dependence of noise arise, at least in part, from different processes. Designs with many choices per participant over a wide range of stakes would allow the individual-differences version of the test to be made properly.

5.2. The magnitude effect is real but smaller than rational inattention implies

Our results also give one of the broadest estimates so far of the magnitude effect itself. Larger rewards were discounted less in 35 of 39 studies, across currencies, procedures and populations, and this held whether the rewards were real or hypothetical and whether testing took place online or in the laboratory. This supports the view that the magnitude effect is a general property of intertemporal choice rather than a feature of particular designs (Green et al., 1997; Frederick et al., 2002; Andersen et al., 2013). The pooled slope of about 0.6-0.7 means that a tenfold increase in the amount lowers the discount rate by a factor of about four to five. At the same time, this slope is clearly below the value of 1 implied by the simplest form of rational inattention, in which the discount rate is inversely proportional to the reward. A smaller slope is not by itself fatal for the broader idea that attention shapes valuation. Versions of the theory in which the cost of attention, or the prior expectation of rewards, changes with the stakes could produce weaker magnitude effects. But the more flexibility is added to the discounting part of the theory, the more the account resembles a descriptive model, and the less it can explain why discounting and noise should be linked. What our results constrain most strongly is precisely this link.

The magnitude effect therefore still needs an explanation. Several existing proposals do not rely on attention to the precision of reward estimates. Value functions that become more sensitive to proportional differences as amounts grow can produce the effect (Prelec and Loewenstein, 1991; Loewenstein and Prelec, 1992). Attribute-based accounts, in which people compare amounts and delays directly rather than computing a discounted value for each option, explain the effect through the way differences are weighed (Scholten and Read, 2010; Dai and Busemeyer, 2014). Other work suggests that larger stakes recruit more self-control (Ballard et al., 2017). Our data cannot decide between these explanations, but they show that whatever explains the magnitude effect on discounting does not need to produce the strong link with choice noise that rational inattention predicts.

5.3. What else might explain choice noise?

If choice noise does not come mainly from imprecise representations of each reward, where does it come from? One possibility is that a substantial part of the noise arises when the options are compared rather than when each reward is represented. Process models of intertemporal choice, in which evidence about amounts and delays is accumulated over time, naturally produce noise of this kind (Dai and Busemeyer, 2014; Rodriguez et al., 2014; Amasino et al., 2019). Eye-tracking studies show that attention moves between options and attributes during a choice and influences which option is chosen (Krajbich et al., 2010; Amasino et al., 2019). Attention may therefore matter for intertemporal choice, but through the comparison process rather than through the precision with which each reward is stored.

A second possibility is that some of the noise does not depend on the stakes at all, such as lapses of attention, response errors or momentary changes in preference. Our models included a lapse rate, and R² used it heavily to absorb its misfit, which suggests that noise that is unrelated to the stakes is an important component. A third possibility is that people's sense of how variable rewards are is formed differently from the running variance assumed in R². Accounts in which values are judged relative to a sample of recently experienced amounts (Stewart et al., 2006; Bhui and Gershman, 2018) and models of efficient coding (Louie and Glimcher, 2012; Polanía et al., 2019) both imply that precision depends on the range of rewards in the current context. Our moderator results are consistent with this idea in one respect: the advantage of the free noise slope was larger in studies with a wider range of amounts.

More generally, our findings fit a growing view that cognitive imprecision is real and important for economic choice, but that its structure must be measured rather than assumed (Woodford, 2020; Khaw et al., 2021; Enke and Graeber, 2023). The models that best described our data were those that let the data decide how noise changes with the stakes. Models that separate the different sources of noise, for example by using response times or eye movements alongside choices, and experiments that manipulate attention directly, are natural next steps.

5.4. Why large, multi-study tests matter

This study also illustrates the value of testing computational theories across many datasets at once. Single studies are limited in their range of amounts, delays and populations, and a model can fit one design well for reasons that do not generalise (Yarkoni, 2022). By fitting the same models to 39 independent studies, we could ask not only whether the theory fails, but also whether it fails everywhere, and whether the failure depends on how the study was run. This approach is similar in spirit to metastudies (Baribault et al., 2018) and to other open databases that pool many experiments (Rahnev et al., 2020). It also shows that a theory can be tested by its own detailed predictions rather than by overall goodness of fit alone (Palminteri et al., 2017).

5.5. Limitations

Our study has several limitations. First, participantspecific magnitude slopes, and therefore the participantlevel correlation between the two magnitude effects, could be estimated only in studies with at least 60 choices per participant. Second, the studies differed substantially in their results, and none of the design features recorded in the database explained these differences after correction for multiple tests; other features, such as sample characteristics, may matter. Third, some large datasets were hard to sample, and their estimates should be read with the convergence flags in mind, although all main conclusions held in well-converged studies. Fourth, R² assumes that the variance of rewards is learned from the amounts experienced in the task; other assumptions about this prior could change its quantitative predictions, although not the absence of a link between the two magnitude effects across participants. Fifth, sex and gender are not recorded consistently across the studies in the database, so we could not test whether the findings differ by sex or gender. Finally, the data were collected for other purposes. Experiments designed specifically to vary the stakes over a wide range within each participant would provide a sharper test.

5.6. Conclusion

Across 39 studies, larger rewards were reliably discounted less, but choices did not become more precise in the way that rational inattention predicts, and the two effects did not move together as the theory requires. The magnitude effect is real and general, and attention may well contribute to it, but a single attentional resource that governs both how future rewards are valued and how noisy choices are does not account for the data. Understanding intertemporal choice will require models in which valuation and choice noise can have different sources.

Ethics statement

This study is a secondary analysis of fully anonymised, publicly available trial-level data from the ITC Database (Pongratz and Schoemann, 2026, 2025). No new data were collected and no participants were contacted. Each original study was conducted by its authors under the ethical approval and informed-consent procedures reported in the original publications. Because only de-identified public data were analysed, no additional ethical approval was required.

For a fixed design and weak discounting, D ij → 1 and ∂ λ α i → γ i /2, while m k,i = γ i . More generally the factor ∑︁ j w ij (D ij -1 2 ) depends on the participant only through D ij , so variation in γ i moves both slopes together; when this factor is similar across participants, as it is in the weak-discounting limit, the two slopes are linearly related and their correlation across participants is ±1.
